sections.h2: Who sets the value that an Ohio tax bill rests on?
sections.html:
Each county auditor appraises the parcels in that county, and the bill is built on the auditor's figure. The Department of Taxation's resource page describes a complete reappraisal on a six-year cycle, with a lighter triennial update in between that leans on sales data instead of a site visit.

A millage rate then converts value into dollars. Inside mills come from local governments without a ballot, and outside mills come from levies voters approved for schools, fire districts and similar services. This explains why a bill can climb while a house keeps its old value: a new levy lifts the rate. Only the value can be contested before the Board of Revision, never the rate.

The Department of Taxation property tax page outlines two ways to question the figure. A number of counties run an informal review, mostly during reappraisal years, and every county accepts the formal complaint. Call the auditor to learn which applies to your parcel.

sections.h2: How are Ohio tax payments scheduled, and what do late ones cost?
sections.html:
Ohio lets a bill be settled in one payment or two. Under R.C. 323.12, a one-time payment is due by the last day of December, while a half payment (plus any older delinquency) is due then and the remainder on June 20 of the next year. Real bills often show later dates, since R.C. 323.17 pushes payment out to January 31 and July 20 whenever the duplicate reaches the treasurer late. Trust the dates printed on your own bill.

The treasurer must receive a payment by the last day, or it must carry a U.S. Postal Service postmark from that day or earlier. Stamps from a private postage meter are no good for this purpose, and a treasurer may hold the books open briefly to process what came in.

The penalty schedule in R.C. 323.121 works like this:

  • Miss the first-half deadline and the unpaid half picks up a ten percent charge.
  • Miss the second-half deadline and the remaining unpaid current taxes pick up another ten percent charge.
  • Back taxes then accrue interest at the rate fixed under section 5703.47.

sections.h2: How do I contest my valuation with the Board of Revision?
sections.html:
Paperwork starts at the auditor's counter, and the auditor hands it on to the Board of Revision. Under R.C. 5715.19 the window closes on whichever comes second: the end of March after the tax year in question, or the day the treasurer finishes collecting first-half payments. Postmarks decide timeliness for mail.

Besides the owner, the statute names the owner's spouse, a retained assessment professional, a retained accountant, appraiser or real estate broker, and in some commercial leases the tenant. Gather comparable sales, an independent appraisal if you hold one, and photographs of the house as it stands.

A repeat complaint is blocked inside one interim period unless something new happened after the lien date. The statute lists what counts:

  • An arm's length sale of the property.
  • A casualty loss of value.
  • A substantial improvement.
  • An occupancy change of fifteen percent or more that hits the property's economics hard.

An unhappy result can go to the Board of Tax Appeals. R.C. 5717.01 gives thirty days from the mailing of the county board's notice.

sections.h2: Which Ohio rules should an owner keep at hand?
sections.html:
Here is a short reference to the sections that matter when a parcel is contested, paid late or sold.

sections.h2: What does the Ohio homestead exemption give a qualifying owner?
sections.html:
It lowers the tax on a home the owner lives in. R.C. 323.152 reaches people who are permanently and totally disabled, people at least sixty-five, some surviving spouses, disabled veterans, and surviving spouses of public service officers killed on duty. Under R.C. 323.151, the protected home takes in as much as one acre around the dwelling, and the age test is met by anyone who reached sixty-four before January 1 of the application year.

The base reduction shields twenty-five thousand dollars of true value, indexed to inflation by the tax commissioner. Disabled veterans and the surviving spouses of officers killed on duty get fifty thousand dollars and face no income test. Other applicants must stay under an income ceiling that the statute states as thirty thousand dollars of total income, also indexed yearly. The auditor can give the current number.

A second layer applies to any homestead. The text lists percentages of the tax from qualifying levies: 5.70 percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, 8.92 percent, 12.15 percent, and then 15.38 percent for the third following year and later. Ask the auditor which step your year falls on.

Filing happens at the auditor's office. The Department of Taxation names form DTE 105A for most people, DTE 105I for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K for officers' surviving spouses. After approval an owner stays enrolled unless eligibility changes. A different benefit, the owner-occupancy credit, covers a primary residence lived in on January 1 of the application year.

sections.h2: How does unpaid tax affect the sale of an Ohio house?
sections.html:
The year's tax lien attaches to the real property on January 1 and stays until tax, penalties and interest are paid, as R.C. 323.11 puts it. Transferring the deed does not wipe it out, so the amount owed must come out of the sale money or the buyer inherits it. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff amount before the closing date.

The deed stage adds a form. Under R.C. 319.202, the buyer files a statement of value with the auditor, and it has to address whether the seller's taxes were reduced by the homestead exemption and whether the land was valued for current agricultural use. A buyer who does not qualify for a reduction the seller enjoyed should expect the next bill to differ.

An owner already behind has an exit from foreclosure. R.C. 323.31 guarantees an occupant owner one written delinquent tax contract with the county treasurer. A home in that position gets up to five years of installments, and at least two if the owner asks. A missed installment or unpaid current tax voids the deal, and none is available while a tax certificate or foreclosure judgment stands.

faqs.q: When is the Ohio Board of Revision complaint deadline?
faqs.a: Whichever is later: the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection ends. Hand the complaint to the auditor, whose office passes it along. If you mail it, the postmark date is what counts.

faqs.q: Does Ohio let me pay property tax in installments?
faqs.a: Yes. The statute allows two halves, one around year end and one in June, and a late duplicate pushes both into January and July. The dates printed on your bill control.

faqs.q: Can I get a homestead exemption if I am under sixty-five?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are permanently and totally disabled on January 1 of the application year, or if you are a disabled veteran or a qualifying surviving spouse. The statute also provides a partial exemption on any homestead. Apply through the county auditor.

faqs.q: Who sets the Ohio millage rate?
faqs.a: Local governments set inside mills, and voters approve outside mills through levies. The rate cannot be changed by a valuation complaint. Only the property's value can be challenged at the Board of Revision.

faqs.q: What if I cannot pay my Ohio property tax on a home I live in?
faqs.a: Ask the county treasurer about a delinquent tax contract. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to one, payable over up to five years. Entering it before a foreclosure judgment keeps the county from filing suit while installments are paid.
